title: The Ten Commandments Spoken Again at Moab
summary: Moses gathers all Israel on the plains of Moab and repeats the Ten Commandments that God spoke out of the fire at Horeb, insisting that the covenant was made with the generation standing in front of him. He then recalls how the terrified people begged him to stand between them and God, and how God approved their request and gave Moses the rest of the commandments to teach them.
story: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell. Israel has spent forty years in the wilderness, the generation that left Egypt has died, and their children are camped east of the Jordan, about to cross into Canaan without him. Chapters 1 to 4 looked back over the road from Horeb, and 4:44-49 introduced a second, longer address. Chapter 5 opens that address by returning to its foundation: the covenant made at Horeb (Deuteronomy's usual name for Mount Sinai) and the Ten Commandments at its center. Everything that follows, the long call to love God in chapters 6 to 11 and the detailed laws of chapters 12 to 26, is built on this chapter. Moses is not simply reciting history. He is binding a new generation to the same God and the same words before he dies.
historical:
The book presents itself as Moses' speeches on the plains of Moab in the fortieth year after the exodus (1:3-5). When that was depends on the date of the exodus, which is debated: some place it in the fifteenth century BC, many in the thirteenth. How the book reached its final form is also debated. Jewish and Christian tradition received it as the words of Moses. Since W. M. L. de Wette's study of 1805, many scholars have linked Deuteronomy, or an early form of it, with the book of the law found in the temple in the reign of King Josiah of Judah, about 622 BC (2 Kings 22 to 23), and see the book as shaped during the seventh and sixth centuries. Others argue that its core is much older and that later scribes preserved and updated Mosaic material rather than composing it.

On every view, Deuteronomy is built like an ancient treaty between a great king and a subject people. Hittite treaties of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BC typically name the king, recount his past kindness to the vassal, list stipulations, provide for the text to be stored and read aloud, call witnesses, and end with blessings and curses. Assyrian loyalty oaths of the seventh century, such as the succession treaty of Esarhaddon (672 BC), share many of these features, especially the curses. Kenneth Kitchen and others have stressed the Hittite parallels, while Moshe Weinfeld and others have stressed the Assyrian ones. Chapter 5 reads like the heart of such a document: the great king names himself and his act of rescue (verse 6), then lays down the basic terms of loyalty.
cultural:
Two differences between this version of the commandments and the one in Exodus 20 open a window on Israel's world. In Exodus the Sabbath command begins “Remember the Sabbath day” and rests on creation, since God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh (Exodus 20:11). Here it begins “Observe the Sabbath day” and rests on the exodus: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (verse 15). In the ancient Near East, rest was something the powerful enjoyed at the expense of those beneath them, and Mesopotamian stories even describe humanity being created to take over the gods' labor. The Sabbath broke that order once a week. The command reaches past the head of the household to sons and daughters, slaves, animals, and the resident foreigner (the ger, an outsider living in Israel without land or clan), and it states its aim plainly: “so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do.” A people who had been slaves were forbidden to become masters who never let anyone stop.

The second difference is in the last command. Exodus names the neighbor's house first and lists his wife among his household; Deuteronomy gives the wife a sentence of her own, adds his field, and uses a second verb, meaning to crave, for his property. Some see a higher view of the wife here, and others see the concerns of a people about to hold farmland. Either way the command reaches inward. Ancient law collections such as Hammurabi's regulated acts a court could see. No court can convict a desire, yet Israel's covenant ends by naming one.
literary: The chapter is a frame around a quotation. Moses speaks in verses 1 to 5 and 22 to 33; in between, God speaks in the first person, addressing each Israelite as a singular you. The commandments (called in Hebrew the ten words, 4:13 and 10:4) fall into two parts, duties toward God (verses 6 to 15) and duties toward neighbor (verses 16 to 21). The first part is expansive, with reasons and motives attached. The prohibitions of murder, adultery, and theft are two Hebrew words each, and in Deuteronomy the last five commands are joined by the word and, binding them into one fabric. Traditions number them differently: Jewish tradition counts verse 6 as the first word and joins other gods and images as the second; Roman Catholic and Lutheran churches, following Augustine, join those two and divide the coveting command; most Orthodox and Reformed churches count other gods and images separately. The narrative after the commandments explains why the rest of Deuteronomy exists: the people could not bear God's voice, so Moses received the remaining statutes alone and now passes them on. The chapter closes with the picture of a straight road with no turning to the right or the left, an image the book returns to often.

outline.t: Moses recalls the covenant made at Horeb
The LORD who rescued Israel; no other gods and no idols
The LORD's name not taken in vain
The Sabbath, rest for the whole household
Parents, life, marriage, property, truth, and desire
The people's fear and their request for a mediator
God approves, and Moses receives the rest of the law

doctrines.note: The covenant is not a relic. Moses insists that God made it “with all of us who are alive here today” (verse 3), though most of his hearers were children or unborn at Horeb. Each generation stands at the mountain again and must answer for itself.

The commandments begin with grace: before any demand, God names himself as the one who brought Israel out of slavery (verse 6). Obedience is a response to rescue, not the price of it. The law then covers the whole of life, from worship to speech, rest, family, marriage, property, testimony in court, and desire.

God makes himself known by speaking. Israel heard a voice out of fire, cloud, and darkness but saw no form (compare 4:12). The two tablets written by God make that spoken word permanent and public, a text that can be kept, read, and taught.

The opening commands forbid both other gods and images of the LORD himself. God calls himself “a jealous God” (verse 9), language drawn from the exclusive love of marriage rather than from petty envy.

words.note: Berit, covenant: a binding relationship sealed by oath, with obligations and consequences on both sides. The Hebrew idiom is to cut a covenant (verse 2), probably from the rite of cutting animals when oaths were sworn (compare Genesis 15 and Jeremiah 34:18). In Deuteronomy the word names the whole relationship between the LORD and Israel, with the Ten Commandments as its core terms (4:13).

Qanna, jealous. This form of the word is used only of God, and always where the worship of other gods is in view. It is the jealousy of a husband who will not share his wife's love with a rival, which is why the prophets later picture idolatry as adultery. It describes zeal for an exclusive relationship, not insecurity.

Shabbat, Sabbath, related to a verb meaning to stop or cease. It is a day defined by what does not happen: no work for anyone in the household. Deuteronomy grounds it in the exodus, making it a weekly memorial of release from slavery, while Exodus 20 grounds it in creation. The two reasons belong together, since the God who made the world is the God who frees his people to rest in it.

Chamad, to desire or covet. The verb can describe desire that is good (Psalm 19:10 uses it of God's judgments being more desirable than gold), but here it is desire fixed on what belongs to someone else. Some interpreters argue that it often includes the scheming that leads to taking (compare Micah 2:2); others hold that it names the inward desire itself. Either way the command reaches beneath outward acts.

christ: The chapter points toward Christ first through the figure of the mediator. The people ask Moses to stand between them and God, and God approves: “They have done well in all that they have spoken” (verse 28). Deuteronomy 18:15-18 recalls this very scene at Horeb when it promises a prophet like Moses, and the New Testament identifies Jesus as that prophet (Acts 3:22-23). Hebrews 12:18-24 sets the fire, darkness, and terrifying voice of Sinai beside Mount Zion, where believers come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The chapter also carries a longing. God says, “If only they had such a heart to fear Me” (verse 29), and the rest of the Old Testament wrestles with that missing heart until God promises to circumcise it (30:6) and write his law on it (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Jesus did not set these commandments aside. He quoted them (Mark 10:19), summed them up as love for God and neighbor, and pressed them inward to anger and lust (Matthew 5:21-30), much as Deuteronomy's own last command presses inward to desire.

hard.q: Does God punish children for the sins of their parents?
hard.a: Verse 9 speaks of God “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me.” Read alone, that sounds like inherited guilt, yet Deuteronomy forbids courts to execute children for their fathers' crimes (24:16), and Ezekiel 18 insists that each person answers for his own sin. Interpreters hold these together in several ways. Many Jewish and Christian readers stress the closing words, “of those who hate Me,” and take the verse to mean children who carry on their parents' rebellion. Others note that three or four generations is the size of an extended household living under one roof in ancient Israel, so the verse describes how a family's idolatry damages everyone in the house within a single lifetime. Still others point to the contrast with verse 10: judgment reaches three or four generations, but loving devotion reaches a thousand. On any of these readings the verse is less a rule of inheritance than a warning about how far sin spreads, set beside a promise that mercy spreads much further.

questions: The commandments begin with what God has done before they say what Israel must do. How does it change obedience to see it as a response to rescue rather than a way to earn favor?
The Sabbath command protects servants, foreigners, and even animals from endless work. Who depends on your willingness to stop, and who bears the cost when you never do?
The people asked for someone to stand between them and God. Why might nearness to God be both longed for and feared?
